title: Officer cleared in fatal shooting: Victim's wife agrees with decision
article: A Calgary police officer will not face criminal charges for shooting and killing a Sikh man armed with a knife in January, according to a report released Monday by the special prosecutions branch of Alberta Justice.

And that's fine with the man's widow, Kuldeep Kaur Cheema. She told the Herald Monday she agrees Const. Ian Vernon was justified in shooting her husband, Harjinder Singh Cheema, after he had violently attacked her and her mother on Jan. 21.
"It was my husband that was wrong," said Kuldeep. "If he didn't shoot him, he could've come back and killed me. Now I'm not scared. I'm safe now."

Acting Calgary police chief Jim Hornby said the report "absolved our officer of any wrongdoing," clearing the way for an internal professional standards review and fatality inquiry to be conducted by a provincial court judge.
"We're pleased to see our reputation has been reaffirmed with the community and the fact that we operated appropriately," said Hornby.

The shooting, captured by a Global News cameraman, occurred after Harjinder, covered in blood and wielding a knife, walked out of his house and onto the street in Queensland Circle, approaching police who had guns drawn.
Harjinder, who had previously been charged with assaulting his wife in August, was shot after he refused to drop the knife.
Before police arrived that day, Harjinder had violently attacked Kuldeep, who has still not returned to work at the Lilydale Poultry processing plant due to her injuries.
"I'm not feeling well," the 25-year-old Kuldeep said Monday. "I get headaches, so I can't wear my hard hat, and I feel pain, especially in my back."
Her mother, Manjit Kaur Toor, 45, underwent surgery on her left hand after the assault, and also has not been able to return to work. She had a job cleaning office buildings.
Kuldeep said her greatest concern has been for her 21/2-year-old daughter, Manveer, who has only recently started sleeping through the night again, more than four months after the shooting.
"She was so scared, she couldn't sleep," said Kuldeep. "She would always be dreaming that someone wanted to kill her."
The fatal shooting was the seventh by Calgary police since 1982, including the October 2003 shooting by Const. Ira Macumber, who killed Deng Fermino Kuol after Kuol slashed him with a knife.

"There's probably been too many of these," said Stephen Jenuth, president of the Alberta Civil Liberties Association. "I think when you have that many, you have to look at the police use of firearms."
A fatality inquiry into the Kuol shooting is scheduled to begin this summer.
Jenuth, a Calgary lawyer, said that while investigations of police shootings try to be exhaustive and impartial, they aren't flawless.
"They tend to be relatively thorough," said Jenuth, "but they start from the perspective that they don't want to find their own officers guilty."
Hornby said the investigations by the province's special prosecutions branch are very comprehensive.
He also said that any officer involved in a shooting can end up very traumatized by the incident and all are offered time off and counselling.
"I make no bones about it, these (shootings) are very difficult and trying for officers involved," said Hornby. "There's a fair bit of work needed to get them through it."
